questions.prompt: What is a retain cycle in Swift?

options.text: Two or more objects holding strong references to each other, preventing deallocation.
options.explanation: Right. Mutual strong references prevent counts from ever dropping to zero.

options.text: A loop statement that iterates over collections repeatedly without an exit.
options.explanation: A retain cycle is about memory references, not infinite iteration loops.

options.text: A compiler error thrown when classes inherit from more than one superclass.
options.explanation: Swift does not support multiple class inheritance.

options.text: A runtime mechanism that compresses unused heap objects into disk cache.
options.explanation: Retain cycles prevent memory cleanup rather than compress heap objects.

questions.prompt: What consequence occurs when a retain cycle exists in an iOS app?

options.text: The Swift compiler refuses to produce an executable application binary.
options.explanation: Retain cycles are runtime occurrences, not compile-time errors.

options.text: Memory is leaked because the affected objects are never freed from the heap.
options.explanation: Right. Leaked objects accumulate and waste device RAM.

options.text: All network requests associated with the instances fail immediately.
options.explanation: Network calls still run; the problem is lingering heap memory.

options.text: The app terminates with an unhandled exception upon launching.
options.explanation: Retain cycles silently leak memory and do not crash on launch.

questions.prompt: Why does a stored closure property accessing `self.title` cause a retain cycle?

options.text: Because string properties cannot be read inside Swift closures.
options.explanation: Closures can read string properties freely.

options.text: Because ARC forbids closures from being stored as class properties.
options.explanation: Storing closures in properties is standard Swift practice.

options.text: Accessing any property on self captures the whole instance strongly by default.
options.explanation: Right. The instance holds closure strongly, and closure captures self strongly.

options.text: Because stored closures execute exclusively on background threads.
options.explanation: Closures execute on whichever thread invokes them.

options.text: [copy self]

options.text: [static self]
options.explanation: Static is a declaration modifier, not a capture list option.

options.text: [weak self]
options.explanation: Right. [weak self] ensures the closure captures self as a weak reference.

questions.prompt: Why do standard collection methods like `items.forEach { ... }` not cause retain cycles?

options.text: They take non-escaping closures that execute and discard references immediately.
options.explanation: Right. Non-escaping closures do not persist after the function returns.

options.text: Swift automatically converts all closures in collection methods into structs.
options.explanation: Closures remain reference closures; lifetime determines cycle risk.

options.text: The compiler disables ARC tracking while iterating over Swift arrays.
options.explanation: ARC remains fully active during collection iterations.

options.text: Array iterations always execute inside a background thread pool.
options.explanation: Standard collection methods execute synchronously on the current thread.

options.text: It forces self to remain alive forever after the closure finishes.

options.text: It safely unwraps self for the closure scope or exits if deallocated.

questions.prompt: Explain what a retain cycle is and how it leads to memory leaks in Swift apps. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a retain cycle occurs when two or more instances hold strong references to each other.
Notes that reference counts never drop to zero, preventing ARC deallocation.
Mentions that leaked memory remains allocated on the heap for the app session.

questions.modelAnswer: A retain cycle occurs when two or more class instances hold strong references to each other. Because each instance keeps the other alive, their strong reference counts never drop to zero. As a result, ARC cannot free their memory, creating a permanent memory leak in the app.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: Explain how stored closures capturing `self` cause retain cycles, and how `[weak self]` resolves this. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that the instance holds the closure strongly and the closure captures self strongly by default.
Explains that adding [weak self] captures self without incrementing its strong reference count.
Mentions that weak self becomes nil if the instance deallocates first.

questions.modelAnswer: A retain cycle forms when an instance stores a closure property and the closure references `self`, creating mutual strong references. Adding `[weak self]` in the closure capture list breaks this cycle by not incrementing the strong reference count of `self`. If the instance deallocates, the weak reference safely becomes `nil`.

sources.title: The Swift Programming Language: Automatic Reference Counting

questions.prompt: Why do standard non-escaping closures like `map` or `forEach` not require `[weak self]`? Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that non-escaping closures execute synchronously within the immediate stack frame.
States that the closure does not outlive the calling function and is discarded after execution.
Concludes that because the closure is not stored, no circular reference can form.

questions.modelAnswer: Non-escaping closures like `map` or `forEach` execute synchronously within the current function call on the stack. They are never stored as properties and do not outlive the function return. Because the closure is immediately discarded, no persistent strong reference can form, making `[weak self]` unnecessary.

Another effective method is adding `print` statements inside `deinit` to verify that view controllers deallocate when popped from navigation. If `deinit` fails to log, a retain cycle is present.

questions.prompt: Explain how the `guard let self else { return }` pattern operates inside a `[weak self]` closure. Answer in 2 to 4 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that guard let self checks if self is still non-nil when the closure runs.
Explains that it creates a temporary local strong reference for the closure execution duration.
Notes that if self has already deallocated, the closure returns early and safely.

questions.modelAnswer: The `guard let self else { return }` pattern checks if the weakly captured `self` is still alive when the closure is called. If `self` has deallocated, the guard exits early to prevent executing logic on dead state. If `self` exists, it creates a temporary local strong reference on the stack that guarantees `self` stays alive until the closure finishes.
